First thing the next morning I took one of them out of the tumbler, and having pierced it with a pin, which I stuck into the wood of the table, I painted it.

It was four <term>lignes</term> <gloss>lines, an old French measure equal to one twelfth of an inch</gloss> wide and eleven and a half long, including the hood of three lines that covered its head.

Four wings extended over its body. The two upper ones were of a fine velvety black, with a stripe of golden yellow near the outer edge. This stripe ran from the neck to two thirds of the length of the wing. The hood was entirely of the same colour, except for a large black spot in the middle, near the neck. This hood followed the movements of the head, which was rounded, and served it as a helmet: it projected by one line all around. Two black antennae, as slender as a fine hair and three lines long, were set on the front of the head, above two black eyes that protruded little and resembled the seed of Amaranth. Three small legs, likewise black, came out from each of the two sides of the body, which in this part was entirely covered with small, fine, very short hairs, and

Thus the poison of death began to work its quality <note>original: "qualificiren", Boehme's word for a force becoming active and making its nature felt</note> in Mercury, and the source of wrath became burning in the eternal Mars, and the dark impression of the property of eternal Nature took him captive. In the dark impression, in the poison of the kindled Mercury, his body became earth, and an enmity against God. It was all over with him, and there was no counsel with any creature, neither in heaven nor in this world; grim death had taken him prisoner in soul and body.

Now how did God go about curing him and tincturing him again <note>to tincture is an alchemical term: to penetrate a substance with a power that restores and ennobles it</note>? Did He take something foreign for it? No, He took the likeness, and cured him with that which had been corrupted in him, namely with the divine Mercury, and with the divine Venus, and with the divine Jupiter. Understand: in man was the expressed Word, which I call the eternal Mercury in man, for it is the true guiding life. It was breathed in, or spoken in, to the human image which God created out of His own being into an image after God, as into a creaturely image. That was the soul with the property of all three worlds: namely with the world of light and understanding, which is God, and with the fire-world, which is the

<summary>Boehme describes how Adam's imagining into the Serpent's property kindled the poison of Mercury and the wrath of Mars, leaving him captive to death in soul and body. God cured him not with anything foreign but with like for like: the divine Mercury, Venus and Jupiter, the expressed Word breathed into man as a soul bearing the property of all three worlds.</summary>

and these are the four statues <note>original: "Statuen", here in the sense of the four standing supports of the world, that is, the four elements</note> of the world, which at the creation of the world were separated out of the Chaos by the divine Wisdom. By their contrary workings they hold this fabric of the world in balance and proportion, and through the inclination of the heavenly powers they bring forth all things beneath and above the earth. Of these we shall speak in the proper place. Here we will proceed to our purpose, and first to the nearer element, that of Earth.

---

### Of the
# Element of Earth.

The Earth is an element worthy enough in its quality and dignity. In this element the other three rest, and above all Fire. It is the most excellent element of all for concealing and for revealing those things that are entrusted to it. It is dense and porous; heavy with respect to its smallness, but light with respect to its nature. It is also the <term>Centrum</term> <gloss>centre</gloss> of the world, and of the other elements as well: through its midpoint passes the <term>Axis</term> <gloss>axle</gloss> of the world, running to both <term>Poli</term> <gloss>poles</gloss>. It is porous, as we have said, like a sponge, which

<summary>The page closes the general account of the four elements, separated from Chaos by divine Wisdom and holding the world in balance by their opposing actions. It then opens the chapter on Earth, described as the resting place of the other three elements, the centre of the world, and a porous body like a sponge.</summary>

learn so many histories that you relate; read so many books that you cite to us; learn so many different languages in which they are written! A thousand years of life would not be enough for it....

It is not necessary, said the doctors, that you should acquire so much knowledge: we have it for you....

But you yourselves, replied the simple men, with all your knowledge, you are not in agreement! What use is it to possess it?

Besides, how can you answer for us? If the faith of one man can be applied to many, what need have you yourselves to believe? Your fathers will have believed for you; and that will be reasonable, since it is for you that they saw.

And then, what is it *to believe*, if *believing* has no influence on any action? And on what action does it have influence, for example, *to believe the world eternal or not?*

It offends God, said the doctors. Where is the proof of that? said the simple men. — *In our books*, answered the doctors.

<summary>The simple men object that no lifetime could master the histories, books and languages the theologians invoke, and that the learned themselves disagree. They ask how one man's faith can stand in for another's and what believing means if it changes no action; the doctors can only answer that the proof lies in their books.</summary>

carefully, it must fester from this wound. So it happens to a person as well. When he has fought off sins and has overcome them, then the little dogs come, against which he does not think to guard himself. These are playmates, or company, or trinkets, or people's pastimes, and people's kindness. They tear at him here and there, and pull at his heart and his inwardness, so that he must of necessity decay in all godly life and in godly earnestness, and no longer feels God's grace and devotion. This small temptation is often far more harmful to a person than the great assaults; for against these he guards himself diligently and holds them to be wrong, but these small failings he will not heed, nor hold them to be wrong. In the same way that all things which one does not recognize are far more harmful than those which one does recognize, so too is this danger, of which one thinks little and takes little heed: companionship, society, or delight in creatures. Now as the deer is heated by every chase, and its thirst grows all the more because of it, so a person should be heated all the more by every temptation with divine love toward our Lord, and should be roused or driven in true thirst by every assault to run more and more into God, where he finds nothing but truth, joy, righteousness and comfort. *)

Now the hunters sometimes do this: when the deer is too weary and too parched, they feed the hounds a little, and so these are held back. When they are sure of the deer in the deer park, they let the deer walk about a little, so that it is somewhat strengthened by this, and then it can endure the hunt all the better. Our Lord does the same to a person. When He sees that the chase is becoming too much for him, and the assault too great, He holds it back a little, and then a drop falls into the mouth of the person's heart, that is, a sweet taste of the sweetness of divine things. This strengthens him so greatly that all things that are not God taste bitter and repugnant <note>original: "widerzehme", which the editor glosses as "widrig", meaning contrary or distasteful</note> to him, and then it seems to him that he has overcome all his distress entirely.

---

*) Ed. 1543.

<summary>Tauler continues his allegory of the hunted deer: after the great hounds of serious sin come the little dogs of company, pastimes and attachment to creatures, which do more harm because no one guards against them. Every temptation should drive the soul to thirst more for God, and God, like hunters resting a weary deer, sometimes holds back the chase and gives a drop of divine sweetness.</summary>

<margin>Twelfth experiment; this effect goes so far as to cause the loss of speech.</margin>
Mr. Jumelin <note>A physician who practised a form of magnetism of his own, independent of both Mesmer and Deslon, and who made his patients available to the Commissioners.</note> had spoken to them of a young lady, aged 20, whom he had caused to lose her speech by the power of <term>Magnetism</term>; the Commissioners repeated this experiment at his house, and the young lady consented to lend herself to it & to let her eyes be blindfolded.

At first an attempt was made to obtain the same effect without magnetizing her; but although she felt, or believed she felt, effects of Magnetism, it was not possible to strike her imagination strongly enough for the experiment to succeed. When she was really magnetized, her eyes still being left blindfolded, there was no more success. The blindfold was taken from her eyes; then the imagination was shaken at once through sight & through hearing, and the effects were more marked; but although her head began to grow heavy, although she felt a discomfort at the root of the nose, & a great part of the symptoms she had experienced the first time, nevertheless her speech was not lost. She herself observed that the hand which was magnetizing her at the forehead needed to come down opposite the nose, remembering that the hand had been so placed when she lost her voice. What she asked was done, & in three quarters of a minute she became mute; nothing more was heard but a few inarticulate & muffled sounds, despite the visible efforts of the throat to push out the sound, & those of the tongue & lips to articulate it. This state lasted only one minute: one sees that, finding herself in precisely the same circumstances, the seduction of the mind & its effect upon the organs of

<summary>The Commissioners report their twelfth experiment, made at Mr. Jumelin's house on a twenty-year-old woman said to lose her speech under Magnetism. Blindfolded, she did not become mute whether magnetized or not; she lost her voice only once she could see and the magnetizer's hand was placed where she remembered it, which points to imagination as the cause.</summary>

<header>Description of Lima, City of the Kings.</header>

<margin>
Form of the city of Lima.
</margin>
In this city there are good houses, and some very fine ones with little towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are broad, all running straight onto the market, from where one can also see into every corner, and on both sides the open country; and through the greater part of the houses run canals, bringing fresh water from the river, to the very great convenience and comfort of the citizens, who can by this means water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they keep fair and pleasant. Also

<margin>
Many water mills, with which they grind their grain.
</margin>
there lie on this river many water mills after the fashion of our country, on which they grind their grain. In sum, very rich citizens live here, some of whom have 150 thousand ducats. And from this city ships sail at times worth 800 thousand ducats, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain on which stands a crucifix. On another side, outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their cattle, and their dovecotes, their vineyards, though with no good grapes, on account of the nature of the land, and fine gardens, not only full of all kinds of fruits of that country, but also

<margin>
Description of the fruitfulness of the land.
</margin>
of the Spanish ones, such as figs, pomegranates, lemons, citrons, oranges, melons, beans, peas and sugar canes, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. And truly, for passing human life in joy, were it not for the scandalous discords and wars there, this place is assuredly one of the fairest in the whole world: for the country thereabouts is so temperate that the whole year through there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. Nor has it ever been seen that famine or plague was there, or any rain or thunderclaps, or lightning struck from heaven;

<margin>
From what the City of the Kings got its name; and it was built in the year 1535.
</margin>
but on the contrary there is always a bright, clear and fair sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535, and is named the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Three Kings' Day <note>Epiphany, 6 January; the Spanish name was Ciudad de los Reyes</note>. As regards provisions, besides the fish, which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as also meat and the fruits of the trees and of the earth, as has been said, there is no less an abundance of wheat and grain; and during the four months when it is summer in Spain it is winter there, and a little colder than at other times. In these 4 winter months there falls every day before noon a light dew or mist like fog, yet not unhealthy as it is with us: for those who have pain in the head, washing themselves with it, obtain relief. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase more in people and in wealth, although for many years there have been over 500 houses there,

<margin>
The breadth and length of the houses of Lima.
</margin>
and the city is laid out very widely, so that a good 2000 could stand there; for the streets are broad and the market square large. Each house has 80 feet of plot and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable timber there to make upper floors from, for it is eaten away by the worms within 2 or 3 years, the houses are built of no more than one storey, and yet very

<margin>
Form of the houses.
</margin>
costly and magnificent, with many chambers, halls and small parlours, fit to live in and to lodge foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials which they bake together very thick <note>that is, sun-dried or baked bricks, adobe</note>, and they fill them with earth. They roof their houses with painted mats or painted linen, and round about and above

<column-break/>

on the walls they make little arbours of reeds in which they shelter from the sun. They need not concern themselves about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under it all these towns where bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, La Paz, La Plata, Trujillo, Guanuco, Chachapoyas, Puerto Viejo <note>original: "Portus vetus"</note>, Guayaquil, Popayán, Catchi, San Miguel, San Francisco. It has been said above that Peru is divided into three kinds of country: into flat land by the sea, into mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and into land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea we have treated until now, beginning from the Line <note>the Equator</note> and Cape Passao up to here. It is further to be known that from Tumbes onward, not only as far as Lima but much farther still, the sea coast southward is very dry and full of great waste sandy places, where for a distance of 10 miles it neither thunders, lightens nor rains <note>the transcription reads "die stadt dondert" here, which appears to be a misreading of a negative; the sense is given by the marginal note</note>; but beyond those 10 miles it does, or so much less or more according as the mountains lie from the sea. There are also in this flat land no springs or wells, but only some 4 or 5 standing waters, which are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants sustain themselves with the water from the rivers that come down from the mountains, which take their origin from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from springs, of which there are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers have in part been described above; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 miles from one another, but mostly 7 or 8, by which travellers regulate themselves, because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, to the breadth of a mile, or wider still, sometimes more, sometimes less, according to the lie of the land, there are various fruitful trees and grain fields, which are tilled and sown by the people, and this they may do the whole year through. Around these rivers there also grow many kinds of wild trees, cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes and sedge, etc. And since the Spaniards took possession of the land, they also sow wheat, moistening the land by means of certain canals which they lead out of these rivers. These rivers, because they run swiftly down from high mountains, can hardly be crossed without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who make their journey along the flat land commonly keep so close to the seashore that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and it rains much, it is perilous to travel there, because of the swelling of the rivers that one must cross, either with certain rafts which they have for that purpose, or with a net which they fill tightly with gourds <note>original: "Cauwaerden", calabashes used as floats</note>, on which the traveller must lie stretched out, while one of the Indians swims in front, pulling the net or the raft onward with a cord, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live under huts made of green boughs. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to the knees and beyond, and an outer garment like a cloak. The women wear a gown of cotton to the length of the body; and although the fashion of the clothing is nearly everywhere the same, there is nevertheless some difference in the adornment of the head: for some wear single cords, some braided ones, some of one colour, others of various colours; and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, and all of them different, according to the custom of the country.

## THE SIXTH CHAPTER.

### *The dissection of the internal parts of the Mayfly.* <note>original: "Haft", the Dutch common name for the mayfly or ephemeron</note>

Having briefly described the egg, the worm, its food, its span of life, its outward limbs, and its nature, I could now fittingly treat of its transformation. But since this goes about its work so swiftly that it consists in scarcely anything but the stripping off of two skins and the stretching out of certain limbs, I judge it better, in order to understand all the more exactly the difference between the <term>*Aas*</term> <gloss>"bait", the name given to the larva, which fishermen used as bait</gloss> and the <term>*Haft*</term> <gloss>the mayfly, the winged adult</gloss>, that is, between the worm swimming and the same worm flying, first to describe its internal parts; all the more so since we find these same parts under both forms of this little creature.

velocity of the stone falling from the state of rest may take place in the same order as the diminution and loss of those same degrees, when by an impelling force it is driven back upward to the same height. But if that is so, I do not see how it can be supposed that the ascending stone, as its velocity diminishes and is wholly consumed, could arrive at the state of rest before passing through all the degrees of slowness.

Simp. But if the degrees of greater and greater slowness are infinite, they will never all be consumed; hence such an ascending heavy body will never be brought to rest, but will move on infinitely, always slowing down: a thing that is not seen to happen.

Salv. That would happen, Signor Simplicio, if the moving body were to linger for some time in each degree; but it merely passes through, without staying there beyond an instant. And because in every finite time <note>original: "tempo quanto", a time having some quantity, however small</note>, even the very smallest, there are infinite instants, these are enough to answer to the infinite degrees of diminished velocity. That such an ascending heavy body does not persist for any finite time in any one same degree of velocity is made manifest thus: if, some finite time being assigned, the moving body were found to have the same degree of velocity in the first instant of that time and also in the last, it could from this second degree be driven upward in like manner through as much space again, just as it was carried from the first to the second; and by the same reasoning it would pass from the second to the third, and finally would continue its uniform motion to infinity.

Sagr. From this reasoning it seems to me that one could draw a quite fitting account of the question debated among the Philosophers, namely what is the cause of the acceleration of the natural motion of heavy bodies. For I consider that in the heavy body thrown upward, the force impressed on it by the thrower goes on continually diminishing; this force, so long as it was superior to the other contrary one of gravity, drove the body upward; once the one and the other have reached equilibrium, the moving body ceases to rise any further and passes through the state of rest, in which the impressed impetus is by no means annihilated, but only that excess has been consumed,

<summary>Salviati argues that a stone thrown upward passes through every degree of slowness before reaching rest, spending no more than an instant in each, since any finite time contains infinite instants. Sagredo then begins to suggest a cause for the acceleration of falling bodies: the gradual wearing away of the force impressed by the thrower against gravity.</summary>

§. 21.

In order to gather everything said so far into a single concept, it is first of all necessary to remind readers that we are speaking here not of how experience arises, but of what lies within it. The former belongs to empirical psychology, and even there it could never be properly worked out without the latter, which belongs to the critique of knowledge <note>original: "Kritik der Erkenntniß"</note> and especially of the understanding.

Experience consists of intuitions <note>original: "Anschauungen", Kant's word for the immediate presentations given through the senses</note>, which belong to sensibility, and of judgments, which are solely the business of the understanding. But those judgments which the understanding forms merely out of sensible intuitions are still very far from being judgments of experience. For in the one case the judgment would only connect the perceptions as they are given in sensible intuition, whereas in the latter case the judgments are supposed to say what experience in general contains, and therefore not what mere perception contains, whose validity is merely subjective. The judgment of experience must therefore add something, in a judgment, over and above the sensible intuition and its logical connection (after it has been made general through comparison), something that determines the synthetic judgment as necessary and thereby as universally valid; and this can be nothing other than that concept which, with regard to one form of judgment rather than the other, the intuition as in itself

<summary>Kant reminds the reader that his inquiry concerns what is contained in experience, not how experience arises, which is a matter for empirical psychology. He then argues that a judgment of experience needs something beyond sensible intuition and its logical connection: a concept that makes the judgment necessary and universally valid.</summary>

**The Spirit.** And I would not grow weary of repeating it in every turn of phrase, if I had to fear that you had not yet grasped it, had not yet impressed it indelibly upon yourself. Can you say: I am conscious of external objects?

**I.** By no means, if I take the matter strictly: for the seeing and feeling, and so on, with which I take hold of things, is not consciousness itself, but only that of which I am first and most immediately conscious. Strictly speaking, I could only say: I am conscious of my seeing or feeling of things.

**The Spirit.** Well then, never again forget what you have now clearly understood. In all perception <note>original: "Wahrnehmung"</note> you perceive solely your own state.

That valley surpasses in excellence all those there are in Peru, for which reason all the Inca Kings, from Manco Cápac, who was the first, down to the last, held it as their garden and place of delights and recreation, where they went to refresh themselves from the burden and heaviness that reigning brings with it, with the affairs of peace and of war that perpetually arise. The ancient poets for the most part give Bacchus horns. It is surely remarkable, then, says Spence, that one so seldom sees these horns on his statues. <note>a)</note> He hits upon this cause, he hits upon another: upon the ignorance of the antiquarians, upon the smallness of the horns themselves, which might have hidden away beneath the grapes and ivy leaves, the god's constant headdress. They were an ornament for the brow, which he could put on and take off.
